title: Greensill: $10bn in Funds and the $440m That Went Elsewhere
summary:
Greensill Capital collapse explained from the regulator, parliamentary and Insolvency Service records.

In November 2020, $440m meant to repay a Credit Suisse fund arrived at Greensill Capital and, the Insolvency Service says, was used for other purposes. Four months later the firm was in administration and $10bn of fund money was frozen. Using FINMA's findings on Credit Suisse, the Treasury Committee and National Audit Office reports, BaFin's order, Lex Greensill's own evidence to MPs, Australian court documents and the 2026 disqualification undertaking, we explain how supply-chain finance turned into future claims on weak borrowers, why one insurance letter mattered so much, and who paid. A disqualification undertaking is not a criminal conviction; the SFO's GFG Alliance investigation is not a finding of guilt.

scenes.say: In November 2020, four hundred and forty million dollars arrived at a London finance firm. It was meant to repay a Credit Suisse fund. The fund never got it.

visual.label: received in November 2020, not used to repay the fund

scenes.say: Four months later, the firm, Greensill Capital, was in administration, and ten billion dollars of investors' money was frozen.
Its founder, Lex Greensill, had been a government adviser with a Downing Street pass. A former prime minister lobbied the Treasury on its behalf.

visual.title: Who was involved
items: Lex Greensill: unpaid government adviser from 2011
David Cameron: lobbied the Treasury in 2020
Credit Suisse: ran the funds its clients invested in
visual.src: Civil Service World, 23 Jul 2021; Treasury Committee, 20 Jul 2021; FINMA, 28 Feb 2023

scenes.src: Civil Service World, 23 Jul 2021; Treasury Committee, 20 Jul 2021; FINMA, 28 Feb 2023

scenes.say: In June 2026, five years on, the official record finally said what happened to that money. We'll get to that document. First, the pitch.

visual.title: Disqualification undertaking
lines: Conduct: Greensill Capital (UK), Greensill Ltd, Greensill Capital Pty

scenes.say: Chapter one. The pitch.
Here is the idea Greensill sold. A big company owes its suppliers money, but pays slowly. A financier pays the suppliers early, and collects from the big company later.

visual.text: Get paid now. The buyer pays later.
visual.sub: A financier steps in between supplier and customer
visual.src: Our explanation; Lex Greensill evidence, 11 May 2021

scenes.src: Our explanation; Lex Greensill evidence, 11 May 2021

scenes.say: Done with real invoices from solid customers, it is ordinary, low-risk trade finance.

visual.label: when backed by real invoices from creditworthy buyers

scenes.say: Lex Greensill described his own business to MPs in May 2021.

visual.text: Lex Greensill gives evidence to the Treasury Committee

scenes.say: He told them: "Our business was all about financing receivables and future receivables."

visual.text: Our business was all about financing receivables and future receivables.
visual.by: Lex Greensill, evidence to MPs, 11 May 2021

scenes.say: Future receivables are money a company hopes to be owed, from sales that have not happened yet. Hold on to that word, future. It matters later.

visual.title: Two kinds of 'receivable'
items: Invoice: goods delivered, customer owes money
Future receivable: a sale that has not happened yet

scenes.say: And it grew fast. SoftBank's Vision Fund invested one and a half billion dollars in 2019, and Greensill reported revenue of four hundred and twenty million dollars that year.
Chapter two. Friends in high places.
Lex Greensill's ties to government began in 2011, when he was brought in as an unpaid adviser on supply-chain finance.

visual.text: Brought into government as an unpaid adviser

scenes.say: A government-commissioned review by the lawyer Nigel Boardman later found he had Cabinet Office and Number Ten passes, business cards, a government laptop and a BlackBerry.

visual.title: What the Boardman review found he had
items: A Cabinet Office laptop and BlackBerry
visual.src: Civil Service World, 23 Jul 2021; Cabinet Office, 22 Jul 2021

scenes.src: Civil Service World, 23 Jul 2021; Cabinet Office, 22 Jul 2021

scenes.say: The review wrote: "It is unclear why Mr Greensill was permitted to remain an adviser to government."

visual.text: It is unclear why Mr Greensill was permitted to remain an adviser to government.
visual.by: Boardman review, 2021, as reported by Civil Service World

scenes.say: In 2020, as Covid hit, David Cameron, by then working for Greensill, contacted Treasury ministers and officials. He wanted Greensill to get access to an emergency Bank of England lending scheme.

visual.title: The lobbying
lines: Calls and text messages to Treasury ministers and officials
!Aim: Greensill access to the Covid Corporate Financing Facility
visual.src: Treasury Committee, 20 Jul 2021; PAC evidence, 22 Apr 2021

scenes.src: Treasury Committee, 20 Jul 2021; PAC evidence, 22 Apr 2021

scenes.say: The Treasury said no. A senior Treasury official, Charles Roxburgh, told MPs the application was rejected at the end of March 2020.

visual.label: Greensill's bid for the Covid Corporate Financing Facility

scenes.say: The Treasury Committee later found Mr Cameron's approach showed "a significant lack of judgement on his part". It said ministers and officials behaved with "complete and absolute integrity".

visual.text: ...showed a significant lack of judgement on his part

scenes.say: And Boardman found Mr Cameron had, on occasion, understated the nature of his relationship with Greensill Capital.

visual.title: Two inquiries, two findings
items: Treasury Committee: lobbying rules 'of insufficient strength'
Boardman: Cameron 'on occasion understated' his relationship with Greensill
visual.src: Civil Service World, 23 Jul 2021; Treasury Committee, 20 Jul 2021

scenes.src: Civil Service World, 23 Jul 2021; Treasury Committee, 20 Jul 2021

scenes.say: Chapter three. Ten billion in funds.
Greensill needed someone to buy its finance. Its biggest outlet was Credit Suisse.

visual.sub: Four supply-chain finance funds, the first launched in 2017

scenes.say: Greensill packaged the claims into securities and transferred them to four Credit Suisse funds. By March 2021, clients had put around ten billion dollars into them.
Switzerland's regulator, FINMA, found the bank relied heavily on Greensill to select the claims and to arrange the insurance behind them.

visual.title: Findings on Credit Suisse
lines: Relied heavily on Greensill for selecting claims
!Relied heavily on Greensill for insurance cover

scenes.say: Then the portfolio changed. FINMA found Greensill later transferred future claims, financing some companies of doubtful creditworthiness. Credit Suisse, at first, did not grasp the shift.

visual.label: some financing companies of doubtful creditworthiness
visual.sub: FINMA: Credit Suisse initially did not grasp the change

scenes.say: Inside the bank, a risk manager advised against a bridging loan to Greensill. FINMA says a senior manager overruled him.

visual.title: Inside Credit Suisse, per FINMA
items: Risk manager: advised against a bridging loan
Bank gave FINMA partly false, overly positive statements

scenes.say: FINMA's verdict, in February 2023, was that Credit Suisse "seriously breached its supervisory obligations".

visual.text: Credit Suisse seriously breached its supervisory obligations in this context...

scenes.say: Chapter four. The insurance clock.
Much of the structure rested on one thing: trade credit insurance, which pays out if borrowers fail to pay.

visual.sub: Cover against non-payment by Greensill's clients

scenes.say: Court documents in Australia showed four point six billion dollars of policies, covering some forty clients, were due to expire on the first of March 2021.

visual.title: The policies, per Australian court documents

scenes.say: The insurer, part of the Tokio Marine group, had written in September 2020 that it did not wish to renew.

visual.text: Insurer: 'does not wish to renew' the cover

scenes.say: Greensill asked the Supreme Court of New South Wales to force a renewal. It warned that more than fifty thousand jobs could be at risk. The court refused.

visual.header: Supreme Court of New South Wales · Mar 2021
visual.title: Application to force renewal
lines: Greensill: some clients 'likely to become insolvent'
Greensill: 50,000+ jobs could be at risk

scenes.say: Chapter five. Seven days in March.
What followed took about a week.

visual.label: from the insurance lapsing to administration

scenes.say: On the third of March, Germany's regulator BaFin closed Greensill's German bank to customers, citing an imminent risk of over-indebtedness.

visual.text: BaFin imposes a moratorium on Greensill Bank AG

scenes.say: BaFin said a forensic audit found the bank could not provide evidence that receivables it had bought from the GFG Alliance actually existed.

GFG is the steel and metals group of the businessman Sanjeev Gupta. Britain's Serious Fraud Office opened an investigation in May 2021, covering its financing arrangements with Greensill. Its case page still lists it as open.

visual.title: Serious Fraud Office, GFG Alliance
items: Suspected fraud, fraudulent trading, money laundering
Status on the SFO case page: open, an investigation, not a finding

scenes.say: On the eighth of March, Greensill Capital's UK companies entered administration. The Greensill group's combined liabilities were more than one point six billion pounds.

visual.title: The collapse
visual.src: Insolvency Service, 7 Mar 2024; Insolvency Service, 4 Jun 2026

scenes.src: Insolvency Service, 7 Mar 2024; Insolvency Service, 4 Jun 2026

scenes.say: Earlier that month, Credit Suisse had closed its four funds, with around ten billion dollars inside.

visual.label: in the four Credit Suisse funds when they closed

scenes.say: Chapter six. The four hundred and forty million.
Now back to the money from the start. One borrower in the Credit Suisse funds was Katerra, an American construction company backed by SoftBank.

visual.sub: US construction company, backed by SoftBank
visual.src: Insolvency Service, 4 Jun 2026; Reuters via Claims Journal, 15 Oct 2025

scenes.src: Insolvency Service, 4 Jun 2026; Reuters via Claims Journal, 15 Oct 2025

scenes.say: According to the Insolvency Service, in late 2020 Lex Greensill caused his companies to enter transactions with Katerra that removed legal protections from a Credit Suisse fund's investment.
In November 2020, four hundred and forty million dollars came in. SoftBank had provided it for buying back Katerra notes held by the fund.
Instead, the Insolvency Service says, Mr Greensill caused or allowed it to be used for other purposes. The notes defaulted. The fund lost four hundred and forty million dollars.

visual.title: Where the $440m was meant to go
items: Meant for: repaying the fund's notes

scenes.say: Credit Suisse sued SoftBank in London to recover it. In October 2025 the High Court rejected the claim, finding SoftBank believed in good faith the money would pay noteholders.

visual.label: Credit Suisse's $440m claim against SoftBank
visual.src: Reuters via Claims Journal, 15 Oct 2025; GTR, Oct 2025

scenes.src: Reuters via Claims Journal, 15 Oct 2025; GTR, Oct 2025

scenes.say: Then, on the second of June 2026, days before a six-week trial, the government accepted a disqualification undertaking from Mr Greensill. The government had sought a ban of up to fifteen years. He accepted nine.

visual.title: The director ban
visual.src: Insolvency Service, 7 Mar 2024; Insolvency Service, 4 Jun 2026

scenes.src: Insolvency Service, 7 Mar 2024; Insolvency Service, 4 Jun 2026

scenes.say: An undertaking means he does not dispute certain facts, for the purposes of those proceedings only. It is not a criminal conviction. The ban runs until June 2035.

visual.title: What the undertaking is, and is not
items: Facts not disputed, for the disqualification only

scenes.say: Chapter seven. Who paid.
The fund investors, around twelve hundred wealthy clients, waited years. By mid-2024 more than seven billion dollars had been returned, with nearly two and a half billion still stuck.

UBS, which had taken over Credit Suisse, set aside about nine hundred million dollars to buy investors out at ninety per cent of the funds' value. Credit Suisse expected the wind-down to run until at least 2031.
British taxpayers were exposed too. Greensill made seven government-backed Covid loans, totalling three hundred and fifty million pounds, to companies in the GFG Alliance.

visual.label: seven government-backed loans to GFG Alliance borrowers

scenes.say: The scheme had a limit of fifty million pounds per borrower. The National Audit Office said taxpayers could lose almost three hundred and thirty-five million pounds. Greensill, through its administrators, denies lending outside the rules.

visual.title: Greensill and the Covid loan schemes
lines: Approved up to £400m, max £50m per borrower

scenes.say: Lex Greensill told MPs: "I bear complete responsibility for the collapse of Greensill Capital."

visual.text: Please understand that I bear complete responsibility for the collapse of Greensill Capital.
visual.by: Lex Greensill, evidence to MPs, 11 May 2021

scenes.say: Our analysis. The official findings point to three lessons, and they apply well beyond Greensill.
One. Supply-chain finance is only as safe as what is actually inside it. FINMA found future claims on weak borrowers sitting where investors expected trade finance.

visual.title: Lesson 1: look inside the label
items: Real invoices from strong buyers: low risk
Future claims on weak borrowers: a different product
FINMA: the bank did not grasp the shift at first

scenes.say: Two. One letter can be the whole risk. The insurer said in September it would not renew. The firm lasted about a week after the cover ended.

visual.text: From the non-renewal letter to administration: about six months
visual.src: GTR, 3 Mar 2021; Insolvency Service, 7 Mar 2024; our analysis

scenes.src: GTR, 3 Mar 2021; Insolvency Service, 7 Mar 2024; our analysis

scenes.say: Three. Access is not oversight. Passes, phone numbers and a former prime minister did not stop the Treasury, a court or an insurer from saying no. They just made the fall more public.

visual.label: the Treasury, a court and an insurer all said no
visual.src: Treasury Committee, 20 Jul 2021; GTR, 3 Mar 2021; our analysis

scenes.src: Treasury Committee, 20 Jul 2021; GTR, 3 Mar 2021; our analysis

scenes.say: If this sounded familiar, watch our First Brands episode: another company where lenders discovered too late what their finance really rested on.

visual.sub: $5 billion in sales, $12 million in cash
